title: New French Literary Prize Rewards Books Written with AI
paragraphs: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in creative work, a new literary prize in France has decided to reward books written with the help of AI instead of trying to keep the technology out.

The prize, called the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA, was launched in October 2026 by three French technology entrepreneurs: Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré. It is named after Blaise Pascal, the 17th-century French mathematician and philosopher, whom the organizers describe as the only Western thinker who was both a pioneer of mechanical devices and a master of language.

The prize is open to anyone writing in French, regardless of their nationality or where they live, and authors do not need a publisher. However, their work must not have been published before. Entrants must submit a manuscript together with a technical document explaining exactly how AI was used to help write it. All major AI language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Although there is no prize money, the winner will receive help to get their work published. A jury of five well-known people will choose the winner, who is due to be announced in mid-December 2026.

According to the organizers, the prize is not a technology competition. Instead, they want to explore what counts as a work of literature when a human author and a machine work together. Rather than trying to catch writers who secretly use AI, they believe authors should openly declare their use of the technology, with transparency as the basis for debate.

The prize was launched at a sensitive time for French literature. Since September 2026, the novelist Thélyson Orélien has faced accusations that his book "C'était ça ou mourir" was largely written by AI, and it was removed from the longlist for the Prix Goncourt, France's most prestigious literary award. Orélien has denied that AI wrote the book. Then, in November, Philippe Jaenada, the winner of the 2026 Goncourt, admitted that he had used AI three times while writing his novel, although he described his use as playful and very limited.
According to reports, French law currently neither regulates nor bans the use of AI to write literary works.
